name: Fireclay butler sink
summary: A deep, square, white sink cast in fireclay. Thick walls, a rolled rim and a weir overflow make a sink that takes heat and weight, and it stays in use in kitchens today.

philosophy.core_thesis: A kitchen sink must be deep, heavy and glazed so hard that a pot, a brush and boiling water do not mark it.
design_principles: Cast the sink in one piece of fireclay, with a wall 20 to 30 mm thick.
Make the basin 450 to 600 mm deep in front, so that a large pan fits flat.
Cut a weir overflow, a slot 40 mm wide, at the back of the Belfast type.
Keep the inner corners rounded with a radius of 25 to 40 mm, so that dirt does not stay.
Glaze every face in white, and glaze the inside twice for a hard surface.
Roll the front rim into a bead 30 mm wide, which makes a clean edge.
Set the sink on two brick piers or cantilever brackets, with a gap of about 20 mm to the wall.
anti_patterns: A shallow sink with a thin wall
A sharp inside corner that holds dirt
A pressed sheet steel bowl in the same shape
A coloured glaze that hides the white face
A bright decoration on the front

form.shape: A deep rectangular sink in two types: the London sink with a flat rim and the Belfast sink with a weir overflow.
form.profile: Straight, vertical walls and a flat floor with a slight fall to the waste outlet; the front is plain and square.
form.foot_and_rim: A rolled front rim and a flat back with a tap ledge, and a waste hole of 40 to 50 mm in a recess.
form.proportion: Typical size 600 by 460 mm, or 760 by 455 mm, and 250 mm deep; weight 40 to 60 kg.
rules: Make the front thick and plain, with no ornament.
Slope the floor 1 in 30 to the waste, so that water does not stand.
Leave a flat shelf at the back for 2 taps or a swan neck tap.
Keep the colour white or off-white.

bodies.rule: Use a coarse buff fireclay with grog, which holds a thick cast without warping. The glaze hides the body on the face.

methods: hand fettling of the weir and the waste
dry and sponge the glaze face
forming.joins: The sink is one casting; the taps and the waste are fitted on site with brass parts and a putty seal.
forming.details: A glaze-free foot, a coarse buff back, a maker's stamp on the back, and a small thick drip line under the rim.

glaze.pattern: No pattern. A moulded maker name or size on the back face is the only mark.
glaze.gloss: High gloss, about 75 to 90 GU, on the white faces.
glaze.wear: The glaze crazes at the weir and the corners, and a grey mark of pots appears on the floor of the sink in use.

palette.strategy: White glaze on the face, buff body on the back and base, and dark brass on the tap.

firing.kiln: A coal-fired down-draught kiln, later a gas tunnel kiln, with long and slow cooling.
firing.scale: A factory makes some hundreds of sinks in a week, and a large kiln takes 20 to 30 at a time.
firing.signs: A flat ground base, small stilt marks on the edge, and a thick glaze at the inner corners.

evidence.title: Glazed ceramic sink with a circled overflow hole

emotion.target_response: A calm, working weight: the viewer sees a sink that serves a house, and thinks of a scullery and hot water.

use_cases: a restoration spec for a period house
a prompt for a still-life scullery
avoid_when: the brief wants a thin stainless steel sink
the brief wants a coloured fitted sink

modifiers.how: Add a transfer print and a moulded rim, and change to a lighter earthenware basin.
Spray a coloured gloss glaze on the face and keep the thick cast form.

wall_thickness.note: Fireclay is cast thick: a wall of 20 to 30 mm keeps the sink from warping in the kiln.
